highlights: The euro's decline to a 17-month low against the dollar dominated European session trading on Monday, as mounting concerns over France's deteriorating public finances and political uncertainty spilled forcefully into broader markets. This is not a gentle continuation of last week's soft euro bias. It is a structural escalation. France's public debt has ballooned from a little over 80% of GDP in 2010 to 119% today, with budget deficits reaching 5% of GDP continuing to add to the problem, and the market decided today that the political system's inability to address it is no longer a background risk - it is the primary driver of European assets. Analysts at ING warned in a note that the market could "easily add another 2% in risk premium to the euro" if the bond selloff extended. Renewed political upheaval in Europe and concern over public finances sent the euro to its weakest since May 2025, boosting the dollar's haven appeal and driving Treasury yields up. The dollar found itself in the unusual position of strengthening on the back of European weakness even as its own domestic data narrative shifted in a dovish direction. Friday's September payrolls increased by just 29,000, well below expectations, with the previous two months revised down by a combined 60,000 and unemployment edging up to 4.2%. Following that weaker-than-expected jobs report, CME FedWatch showed a 77.9% probability that the federal funds rate would remain in the 3.75%-4.00% range at the next meeting - a dramatic reversal from the 70.3% hike probability that closed out last week's briefing. The October hike is effectively off the table in the market's current pricing, yet longer-dated Treasury yields hit their highest levels in more than two decades on Monday, with the benchmark 10-year jumping about 7 basis points to 5.347%, its most elevated level since April 2002. The 30-year was more than 7 basis points higher at 5.702%, a level not seen since late May 2002. That is the session's central paradox and it deserves time. Growth stocks rallied because the Fed is now likely pausing. Bonds sold off because the long end is being driven by structural forces that have nothing to do with the next FOMC decision. "That reinforces the idea that the long-end selloff is being driven by more than monetary policy: elevated real yields, heavy borrowing and competition for capital continue to demand a higher term premium," Capital.com's Daniela Hathorn noted. This is the environment where yield-curve watchers matter more than rate-hike watchers, and the distinction carries real consequences for the instruments in this briefing. The US Dollar Index topped 102.50, its highest since April 2025, before the ISM services index eased to 54.9, just under the 55 forecast. Most of the index's slide after the release came from the euro rising back above 1.1200, not from lower US yields, which edged higher. ISM services remains solidly in expansion territory, which limits how far the Fed pause narrative can carry equities if inflation remains sticky - particularly with energy costs elevated. Gold bounced up from two-month lows but remains within previous ranges, below $4,200. High US yields and the risk-averse market amid the global bond selloff are buoying the safe-haven dollar, and bulls need to break the $4,230 resistance area to ease The USD/JPY exchange rate rose to 158.19 on October 5, up 0.21% from the previous session. The pair opened the week near 157.73 and has pushed modestly higher through the day as the dollar's European haven bid and still-elevated US yields overrode the support from Tokyo's inflation data. BREAKING - EUR/USD hit a 17-month low today, driven by French sovereign debt fears and Spain's snap election announcement. This is a structural escalation from last week's 8th-percentile CFTC positioning extreme. The euro touched $1.1161 during Asian trading, after four consecutive weekly losses, and stood at around $1.12 at the European open, recovering slightly. The Dollar Index reached a nearly 18-month high of 102.53 on Monday, with Monday's rise coming mostly in two bursts through the October 1 high near 102.20 to a peak just above 102.50, before giving back about half of that gain, holding above 102.00. The move came as the US dollar strengthened despite weaker-than-expected US jobs data - still-elevated US Treasury yields continued to support the dollar, widening pressure on the euro. The previous briefing's 1.1350 downside target has been comprehensively broken. The 1.1200 level, which was a distant structural reference last week, was tested and briefly breached during Asian hours. The recovery to the 1.12 area at the European open and the bounce after ISM services suggests that 1.1200 is the zone where some buyers are willing to lean - but ING's warning of a further 2% risk premium on top of current levels means 1.1000 cannot be dismissed as a tail outcome if French bond spreads widen further. The French government has presented an ambitious plan to reduce the budget deficit to 5% of GDP by 2027 through 54 billion euros in spending cuts, with Finance Minister Lecornu stating that only adoption of this plan can keep alive the prospect of eventually meeting the EU's 3% target. That plan has a political survival question attached to it that markets are pricing in today. Investors will look to minutes from the Federal Reserve's September meeting, due Wednesday, for clues on the path of interest rates. That is the week's dominant macro event, and it arrives two sessions away. The updated September Summary of Economic Projections showed a distinctly more hawkish policy path than in June: the 2026 federal funds rate median was raised to 4.1% from 3.8%, the 2027 median to 4.1% from 3.6%, and 2028 to 3.9% from 3.4%. A more cautious discussion in the minutes, particularly if officials expressed concern about overtightening or downside risks to growth, could pressure the dollar. Treasury yields could rise further if the minutes reinforce the September SEP's higher projected rate path and reveal that officials discussed further tightening. For this briefing's instruments, the minutes could either validate the current dollar-up, euro-down, metals-pressured setup, or crack it sharply in a single afternoon. The French fiscal story is the key overnight European risk. The French government has presented its draft 2027 budget with 54 billion euros in spending cuts to reduce the deficit to 5% of GDP by 2027. If the parliamentary passage of that budget is questioned overnight by any party leader or ratings agency commentary, EUR/USD's 1.1200 floor becomes very thin. Spain's snap election announcement compounds the political risk premium on the euro zone broadly. Any sign that ECB officials are considering emergency tools - verbal intervention, spread control language - would be the single catalyst most likely to trigger a violent EUR/USD short squeeze from this positioning extreme. Watch for any ECB communication. The EUR/USD breakdown to a 17-month low on French sovereign debt fears - not on a Fed catalyst - confirms that currency markets in 2026 are as much driven by fiscal credibility as by rate differentials. If you were trading EUR/USD short purely from Fed mechanics, you were right for the wrong reason. Understand why your trade is working. The October Fed hike probability collapsing from 70.3% to below 20% in a single week while the 10-year yield simultaneously hit 24-year highs is the most important yield-curve signal of the month: the bond market is telling you that the long end is no longer about the next meeting. Wednesday's Fed minutes are the week's single highest-impact event: they arrive into a market where equity bulls are pricing a pause, bond bears are pricing structural term premium expansion, and dollar bulls are pricing European fiscal collapse - the minutes cannot satisfy all three simultaneously. support@marketsmastered.com

results.title: US Open Market Brief 5 Oct 2026: Hike Fears Faded, Yields Stayed | Samuel & Co Trading
highlights: Friday’s soft jobs report did the Federal Reserve a favour. It did very little for the bond market. Traders have largely stopped worrying about a rate rise this month, yet the US 10-year yield is sitting around 5.28%, close to its highest in years, and that is the weight Wall Street carries into Monday’s cash open. Meanwhile, Treasury yields have refused to celebrate. The 10-year has spent the session between roughly 5.25% and 5.29%, and the 30-year is near 5.64%. Investors are still demanding a hefty premium to hold long-dated US debt, with heavy government borrowing and energy costs keeping that premium sticky. When the risk-free rate is that high, every share price has to work harder to justify itself. This morning’s brief was about cooler US jobs and French political strain pushing the euro lower. Since then, Europe’s worry list has grown. Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election, and the euro touched a 17-month low against the dollar near 1.1162 before steadying around 1.12. The CAC 40 has slipped to a six-month low. Oil has also firmed up a little. WTI has climbed back above $90 to around $90.80, while Brent is up about 0.7% near $103 after reports of another tanker being hit near the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco’s chief added to the nerves by saying it could take two years to rebuild global oil stockpiles. And yields have drifted higher rather than lower through the European session, which is the opposite of what a dovish Fed story would normally deliver. The real contest today is between two forces On one side, softer jobs data has taken a Fed rise off the table for October, which helped push the Nasdaq to a Friday. On the other, the bond market is telling equity that money is cheaper any time soon. Stocks have through all of this, but resilience at a 5.28% 10-year yield leaves less room for disappointment. The dollar is firm, but mostly because Europe is giving it a hand. The dollar index is up about 0.3% near 102.2, with the euro doing much of the heavy lifting on French and Spanish political worries. Sterling is a little softer near $1.322, holding up better than the euro, and the yen is steady near 158 to the dollar. A firm dollar alongside fading Fed hike odds tells you this move is about the rest of the world as much as about America. Bonds are the story beneath the story. The 10-year near 5.28% and the 30-year near 5.64% keep borrowing costs high for companies, homeowners and governments alike. Goldman Sachs’ Gutman has told governments to cut spending if they want to curb runaway borrowing costs, and the debate over fiscal discipline is now running on both sides of the Atlantic. Until long-dated yields ease, any rally in shares is working uphill. For the S&P 500, Friday’s close near 7,723 is the first reference, with futures trading near 7,762. On the Nasdaq, the question is whether Friday’s record high holds as chip stocks cool. In bonds, the 10-year range between 5.25% and 5.29% today is the line to watch, and a break above it would likely weigh on growth stocks. In currencies, the euro’s 17-month low near 1.1162 and the dollar index near 102.5 matter. For commodities, Brent around $100 and gold near $4,200 are the round numbers in play. Our read is that the bias into the open is cautious rather than bearish. The Fed has bought the market some time, but the bond market has not handed back the pressure, and that tug of war usually means choppy trading rather than a clean trend. The evidence is in the detail: futures dipping only slightly, yields stuck near multi-year highs, the dollar firm on European politics and big individual stories such as PTC driving the action. The opportunities are likely to be in single names and sector moves rather than in the index as a whole, while the main risks are a hot ISM services reading that revives rate worries, or a fresh oil scare from the Gulf. What would change the view is a decisive move in the 10-year yield: a drop back towards 5.20% would give equities room to rally, while a push through 5.30% would put Friday’s record under pressure. Markets to watch are the 10-year Treasury, Nasdaq 100 futures, EUR/USD and Brent.

results.title: Global FX Market Summary: USD Surge, French Fiscal Crisis, and Gold’s Yield Tug-of-War Shape Markets, 5 October 2026
highlights: Global FX Market Summary: USD Surge, French Fiscal Crisis, and Gold’s Yield Tug-of-War Shape Markets, 5 October 2026 Strong US dollar and resilient Fed policy contrast with French fiscal turmoil weighing on the Euro, while gold struggles despite geopolitical risks. The US Dollar Index (DXY) has surged toward fresh yearly highs in the 102.50 to 102.85 range, buoyed by the broader resilience of the US economy. Although recent labor market data—specifically September’s Nonfarm Payrolls increasing by a meager 29K alongside an uptick in the unemployment rate to 4.2%—and softer Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation reports have led traders to heavily discount an immediate October rate hike, the greenback remains fundamentally well-supported. Market participants continue to price in a more resilient monetary policy trajectory for the Federal Reserve compared to overseas central banks, keeping the US Dollar firmly anchored as a favored global currency even as benchmark 10-year Treasury yields hover near multi-year highs. French Fiscal Tur Hammer the Euro The single currency has tumbled to multi-month lows, slipping near one-year troughs against the US Dollar and losing ground against the British Pound as severe political and fiscal turmoil takes center stage in France. Surging French 10-year government bond yields, driven by high debt levels, widening budget deficits, and political gridlock regarding the 2027 budget, have amplified Eurozone fragmentation fears and pushed the region’s Sentix Investor Confidence index down to 2.7 in October. While the European Central Bank retains powerful backstops like the Transmission Protection Instrument to limit systemic contagion, the immediate fiscal anxiety in Paris has triggered a broad-based softening of the Euro across major currency pairs. Precious metal prices remain constrained, with Gold (XAU/USD) trading sideways and struggling to sustain momentum above the psychological $4,200 threshold. The non-yielding asset finds itself caught in a persistent tug-of-war between strong downward pressure from elevated US Treasury yields and a dominant US Dollar on one side, and robust safe-haven demand on the other. Lingering geopolitical risks—ranging from active conflicts in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war to energy-driven inflation vulnerabilities—continue to provide a supportive floor for bullion, yet the combination of high borrowing costs and aggressive rate pricing keeps gold tightly range-bound.

results.title: Global Markets Analysis: Geopolitical Volatility Meets Economic Divergence – The World of Pips
highlights: By Siti Muinah Oct 5, 2026 #analysis, #central-banks, #divergence, #economic, #economy, #geopolitical, #global, interest-rates, #macro, #markets, #meets, # The global financial landscape is currently navigating a period of profound complexity, characterized by a stark divergence between bond market volatility and equity market resilience. As we move into the new week, investors are grappling with a dual-pressure environment: a significant cooling in the U.S. labor market that has upended interest rate expectations, and a deteriorating geopolitical situation that is placing renewed pressure on global energy security. While bond markets are reacting with traditional sensitivity to macroeconomic indicators, equity markets—particularly in the technology sector—are exhibiting an unprecedented decoupling from interest rate shocks. This report examines the interplay between these forces, the shifting stance of central banks, and the geopolitical flashpoints currently defining the global narrative. This cooling was mirrored in wage growth, where average hourly earnings rose by only 0.1% month-over-month, missing the 0.3% forecast. Consequently, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%, slightly higher than the 4.1% expectation. The market reaction was swift: the probability of an October rate hike by the Federal Reserve, which sat at approximately 70% last Tuesday, has plummeted to below 20%. The most striking feature of the current market cycle is the disconnect between interest rates and equity valuations. Despite a rapid rise in U.S. 10-year Treasury yields, global equities remain remarkably resilient. Last week, equities closed only 0.5% lower, and over the past two weeks—the period during which most of the yield surge occurred—equities have actually gained 0.4%. This divergence suggests that the market has fundamentally re-evaluated what drives equity returns. We are currently witnessing one of the most robust corporate earnings cycles in modern history. Consequently, the "rate shock" is being treated as a secondary concern by equity investors who remain laser-focused on bottom-line growth. Volatility has effectively been isolated to the bond market, while equities are trading on a separate, earnings-driven trajectory. The aftermath of the U.S. jobs report has left the bond market in a state of flux. While the initial data release provided a temporary reprieve for Treasury prices, the impact was short-lived, with 10-year yields ending the day 2–3 basis points higher than the open. In foreign exchange, the U.S. dollar is displaying renewed strength, moving below the 1.12 level against the euro and breaching 158 against the Japanese yen. The euro remains under pressure, burdened by internal political uncertainty in France, which continues to act as a drag on investor sentiment toward the bloc. As we look ahead, the interplay between the Federal Reserve’s cooling labor market mandate and the rising geopolitical risk premium will remain the primary drivers of volatility. While the bond market is correctly identifying the risks of a shifting macroeconomic environment, the equity market is placing a high-conviction bet on the durability of corporate earnings. For investors, this suggests a need for a tactical approach: bond portfolios should be prepared for continued volatility as the Fed recalibrates, while equity portfolios may continue to find strength in high-growth sectors, provided the current earnings cycle maintains its current velocity. The situation in the Middle East and the potential for energy supply disruptions remain the "known unknowns" that could, at any moment, force a convergence between the disparate worlds of bond and equity sentiment.

results.title: US 10-Year Yield Hits 5.34%, Highest Since 2002, on AI…
highlights: Bond volatility dominates markets as US 10-year Treasury yields rose above 5% and touched 5.34% on 1 October, the highest since 2002, driven by Middle East oil tensions, strong US data and heavy AI-related corporate issuance. Equities proved resilient, with the S&P 500 down 0.3%. Amundi sees a regime shift, expects sustained volatility, credit dispersion and recommends an active, globally diversified fixed income approach with a preference for higher-quality bonds. - Bond volatility has decoupled from equity volatility, with the MOVE index rising significantly while the VIX remains contained. - Higher long-term yields are driven by Middle East oil tensions, stronger US activity data and heavy corporate issuance to finance the AI build-out. - Investors are rotating out of higher-risk bond segments, causing credit spreads to widen and French government bond spreads to widen with a flight to German Bunds. - Amundi recommends an active, globally diversified fixed income approach with a preference for higher-quality bonds, as higher yields improve bond appeal but volatility and dispersion remain elevated. US 10-year Treasury yield peak (1 Oct) 5.34% - Middle East tensions keep oil prices elevated, adding to inflation pressure, especially for Europe. - Rising bond yields and heavy AI-related debt issuance increase scrutiny on corporate balance sheets and could trigger broader credit spread widening. - French political uncertainty and fiscal challenges may drive persistent volatility in French bonds, with spillovers to other peripheral bonds. and added to Bond volatility has become the main feature of recent market moves. Equities have remained relatively resilient, but bond yields have moved higher in a context in which markets are becoming more sensitive to macro data and policy expectations. As yields move higher and news flows evolve, markets are readjusting across countries and curves. Global bond markets have been the first to readjust, but we have recently seen moves in global credit markets too. The moves are being driven by several overlapping forces. Tensions in the Middle East have kept oil prices elevated and added to inflation pressure, while stronger US activity data in recent weeks and heavy corporate issuance linked to the AI build-out have pushed long-term yields higher. While benefiting from solid fundamentals, European bonds are under pressure from risks related to energy prices and inflation, reinforced by some fiscal and political concerns, including in France. For investors, the key implication is the need for a more active approach in fixed income and stronger diversification. Higher yields are improving the appeal of bonds, which now offer yields not seen in decades, but as flows adjust across countries and segments, we see volatility remaining high and dispersion rising in the credit space. In this environment, an active and globally diversified approach to fixed income remains important, with a preference for higher-quality bonds. At the same time, while equities are well supported by strong earnings, prospects for higher inflation and higher yields will increase scrutiny on balance sheets, and on excess capital and debt build-out in the AI ecosystem. This will call for more selection and increase diversification at sector level and across asset classes. Market volatility has increased in recent weeks, particularly in bond markets. The MOVE index, a measure of expected volatility in US Treasuries, has been rising significantly, decoupling from the VIX equity volatility indicator in an unusual move. This is significantly different from the March volatility spike that affected both markets at the start of the Iran war. While equities have remained resilient and continue to be dominated by the AI capex story, bond yields have been rising sharply over recent weeks. The US 10-year Treasury yield was around 4.7% in late August, moved above 5% for the first time since 2023 on 15 September, and briefly touched 5.34% on 1 October, its highest level since 2002, before easing back into the weekend. Major equity markets also saw more marked swings but closed the past week with overall little change (-0.3% for the S&P 500, -1.1% for the STOXX Europe 600). We are seeing a rotation, particularly within bond markets, as investors exit areas of higher perceived risk to reduce overall portfolio volatility. Middle East tensions and the oil outlook. Escalating tensions in the Middle East over the summer, and the lack of clarity around when the war may end, have kept energy markets highly volatile. In recent days, demand concerns and some easing of the most acute fears have pulled prices back, but Brent remains in the $95 to $110 range, well above the $87 average seen between June and August. This weighs especially on European bonds, as Europe is more exposed to rising oil and gas prices. The G7 leaders’ decision last week to release up to 100 million barrels from emergency oil and diesel reserves to ease pressure on energy prices may help to further stabilise markets. Growth, inflation and the Federal Reserve. Long-term yields have moved higher on the back of stronger signals on US economic activity, rising inflation risks stemming from the war and heightened competition for capital from heavy corporate issuance to finance the AI build-out. That is happening against a backdrop of positive earnings results and supportive market sentiment, which has helped risk assets remain resilient, but it has also led investors to demand more compensation for bonds. France and European bond volatility. Rising political uncertainty around the French budget, at a time of increasing debt levels, broader global spillover from higher bond yields and upcoming elections next year, has added another source of volatility in European bonds. As a result, we are seeing a rotation, particularly within bond markets, as investors try to reduce overall portfolio volatility. This is visible in global credit, where corporate bond spreads have recently started to widen. Here, record AI capex and debt issuance have also been a major driver with rising market scrutiny. In European government bonds, we have seen further spread widening in French bonds with spillovers into Italian and other peripheral bonds, and a “flight to safety” into German Bunds. These are, in our view, orderly rotations that are part of the re-adjustment to a backdrop of higher rates and higher inflation risks. We believe the most likely scenario is one of gradual consolidation, which would not fully resolve the medium-term fiscal challenge. The market has already become more watchful on French government debt in recent weeks, given the approaching budget deadline, higher debt-servicing costs and political uncertainty ahead of next year’s elections. Current market pricing reflects this uncertainty, as shown by the widening spread between France’s ten-year government bond yield and Bunds. However, it remains below previous crisis levels, and we see this move driven more by foreign investor outflows than by genuine concerns Bond yields are increasingly attractive, but volatility is likely to stay high, calling for an active approach to bond investing. Bond markets are being shaken by unusual volatility. This reflects a regime shift towards a world shaped by geopolitical ruptures, inflationary pressures driven by demand for investment in AI, the climate transition, and increasing debt. At the same time, recent rises in bond yields are making bonds increasingly attractive to investors, with yields now at levels not seen in decades. In this environment, an active and globally diversified approach to bonds is key. In credit we expect dispersion to rise, as the market reassess the impact of higher rates across different sectors and businesses. Here we maintain a preference for high-quality bonds less exposed to the challenge of rising rates.

results.title: The Bond Market Is Screaming. The Stock Market Can't Hear It.
highlights: Bond volatility just jumped 35% in a month, junk bond spreads are starting to widen, and the VIX is asleep at 15. Credit has called every major stock top since 2007, and it's flashing again. Oct 05, 2026 The stock market’s fear gauge, the VIX, closed Friday at 15.31, near its lowest levels of the year. The bond market’s fear gauge, the MOVE Index, closed the same day at 107.29 after jumping roughly 35% in September. When those two indices disagree this badly, the bond market has usually been right first, and as of last week, credit spreads have started siding with bonds. If you don’t understand the credit markets, you do not understand the stock markets. The 10-year Treasury yield ended 2025 at 4.14% and closed Friday at 5.28%, a rise of 114 basis points in 9 months. Earlier last week it touched 5.34%, its highest level since 2002, and the quarter that ended in September produced the largest quarterly jump in the 10-year yield this century. Chart 1 covers October 2025 to October 2026. The VIX’s closing high this year was 31.05 in late March, when the oil spike tied to the Iran war hit markets. It has made lower highs ever since. The 10-year yield in the bottom panel has done the opposite, climbing steadily from about 4% to new highs. (The chart uses Treasury’s official daily rate, which printed 5.24% on October 2 versus the 5.28% market close.) The Fed made the picture worse. On September 16, 2026, it raised rates 25 basis points to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first hike since 2023, citing energy prices driven by the Middle East conflict. A rate hike does not produce a single barrel of oil. All it did was raise borrowing costs at the short end while long-term yields kept climbing on their own, which tells you the Fed has no control over the part of the curve that sets your mortgage rate. The MOVE Index rose 35% in September through September 28, a monthly jump seen only 8 times since 2008. During the week of September 25 alone, it climbed about 30%, its biggest weekly gain since the April 2025 tariff shock. Chart 3 runs from October 2025 to October 2, 2026, and the two blue lines tell the story. On the MOVE (top panel), the rising line connects higher lows since early July: bond volatility has been building a floor for 3 months, and in late September it exploded off that floor to 107.29. On the VIX (bottom panel), the falling line connects lower highs since June: stock volatility keeps fading. The intermarket chain runs in order: bond volatility rises first, credit spreads widen second, and stocks crack last. Chart 4 shows that order from January 2006 to October 2026. In 2007, the junk bond spread bottomed and started rising months before the S&P 500 peaked in October 2007. In mid-2014, spreads turned higher roughly a year before the S&P 500 topped in May 2015 and fell into its August 2015 and early 2016 selloffs. In the second half of 2021, spreads bottomed again ahead of the January 2022 stock peak. Lenders spotted the stress first every time, because bondholders only care about getting repaid and watch balance sheets more closely than stock buyers do. The high-yield (junk bond) spread widened from 2.93% on September 25 to 3.24% on October 1, a 31 basis point jump in 4 trading days. Chart 5’s top panel shows the all-in yield on junk bonds at 8.22% as of October 1, 2026, breaking above its 12-month average of 7.08%. Companies with weaker balance sheets now pay more than 8% to borrow, and the ones facing large debt maturities in 2026 and 2027 must refinance at those rates or default. Rising rates on revolving credit can have a big negative impact on businesses that don’t make any money or have very small margins. The bottom panel is the price ratio. It divides TLT by HYG (a junk bond ETF) to compare duration risk with credit risk. The ratio has fallen from about 2.5 in 2020 to 1.01 today, meaning investors spent 6 years preferring junk bonds over long Treasuries a trade that works only while spreads stay tight. Spreads are well below the -term average of 5.17%, so they have plenty of room to widen, and a rising MOVE is what historically pushes them there. above its March 26 high near 115 and the spread climbs above 4%, rate stress will have reached balance sheets, and the VIX at 15 will not survive it. The next tests are on October 28 much more long coming. If supply keeps climbing mortgage rates and corporate refinancing costs go higher, and stocks will last asset to reprice Oil: WTI closed at $91 last week and remains stuck below $95 resistance because the dollar’s breakout makes every dollar-priced barrel more expensive for overseas buyers. U.S. dollar: The Dollar Index closed near 102 last week (October 2, 2026), breaking out above its summer highs around 101.75. The sequence behind it starts with the oil shock, which pushed the Fed into a September 16 rate hike, while heavy Treasury borrowing lifted the 10-year yield to 5.28%, the highest since 2002. Those yields now pay far more than bonds in Europe or Japan, so global money is selling other currencies to buy dollars and capture that gap. The stronger dollar squeezes every foreign company and government that has to repay dollar debt, and it's a headwind for commodities because they're priced in dollars and get more expensive for overseas buyers every time the dollar climbs. That pressure is already showing in WTI stalling below $95. Japanese yen: The yen closed at 0.6336 last week (about 158 yen per dollar), and Treasury Secretary Bessent wants it stronger. He called the yen “very undervalued,” backed the first joint U.S.-Japan yen-buying intervention in 28 years in July after it hit roughly 164 per dollar, and keeps pressing the Bank of Japan to raise rates. The rally faded from its September high near 0.6550 because 5.28% U.S. Treasury yields keep paying traders to borrow cheap yen and buy U.S. assets, which pushes the yen lower. That leaves a carry trade built on a currency the U.S. Treasury is actively trying to push higher, and if Bessent and the Bank of Japan force the yen back above that level, those traders have to sell U.S. stocks and bonds at the same time to repay their yen loans.

We are forced to ask a critical question: Is your long-term investing plan well suited for a world of higher and more volatile inflation? And are the assets within it fragile or resilient in the face of the risks? Our view that inflation will be more volatile than before the pandemic, and more susceptible to upward shocks, sets the expectation for a higher correlation between stocks and bonds – and bears strongly in favor of assets that can provide a lower volatility profile than equities but can also perform well in more inflationary environments. Consider the inflationary backdrop before the Middle East conflict began to snarl energy supplies and trigger price surges. Inflation had been sticky. Core U.S. consumer prices and private sector workers’ pay were rising about 1.0 ppt to 1.5ppt faster per year than in the prepandemic period. The core personal consumption expenditure deflator (PCE), the Fed’s preferred metric, accelerated markedly in 2025, and in January 2026, prices had risen 3.1% year-over-year (y/y), above the Fed’s target. In that report, inflation was firm in discretionary consumer services, such as sit-down restaurants and personal care services – categories largely insulated from global supply and tariff effects. Such persistent inflation suggests robust domestic demand and consumers’ willingness to pay higher prices. Meanwhile, the Employment Cost Index, another measure of wage growth, is still above pre-COVID levels. Absent rising household savings, that means faster spending growth, fueling the demand side of inflation. Then the Strait of Hormuz price shock hit, just as inflation was returning to the Fed’s target. 42 Higher fuel costs began flowing through the economy via transportation, logistics and manufacturing inputs, while directly impacting household budgets and inflation expectations. Fed research suggests each sustained $10-per-barrel increase in oil prices raises inflation by roughly 30bps to 35bps. 43 A roughly $40-per-barrel sustained increase in oil prices (above preconflict prices) would imply, by the Fed’s math, nearly a 1-ppt higher inflation rate. 42 Maximiliano A. Dvorkin, Fernando Leibovici and Ana Maria Santacreu, “How Tariffs Are Affecting Prices in 2025,” Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, October 16, 2025. 43 Federal While current inflation dynamics do not look nearly as troublesome as in 2022, the possibility of a repeat bears watching. In 2022, core PCE was running at 5.2% when Russia invaded Ukraine in February, setting off a 60% surge in oil prices. The Fed responded by raising interest rates 425 bps over that calendar year. The S&P 500 ended 2022 down 20%; core fixed income lost 13%. Most portfolios suffered the consequences. Macro hedge funds delivered a 9% return – one of the only asset classes to withstand the hiking cycle. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) could be forced to make a difficult choice: Maintain its easing bias (as several members, the treasury secretary and the president clearly prefer) and risk stoking even more inflation and higher long-term bond yields, keep rates steady or pivot back toward rate hikes that risk destabilizing financial markets, at a time when stress is building in certain pockets of credit. History suggests that central bank rate hikes in response to an energy price shock are classic precursors to recession. 44 Maintaining purchasing power is a core goal for many investors and families. Higher inflation makes achieving that goal more difficult. It erodes real wealth faster, and higher inflation is associated with higher correlations between stocks and bonds, which increases the fragility of a traditional portfolio. We believe that hedge fund strategies, such as relative value and macro, can help reduce overall portfolio risk due to their limited correlations to both stocks and bonds. Certain liquid alternatives deliver similar active strategies. Macro hedge funds proved resilient in 2022 when stocks and bonds both took significant losses. According to our data, U.S. Private Bank clients are typically under allocated to the asset: 94% of clients do not own hedge funds in their portfolios. 61

High yield (HY) spreads measure the extra yield investors demand to hold bonds rated below investment grade, BB+ and lower by S&P, Ba1 and lower by Moody's, compared to US Treasury bonds of similar maturity. results.title: The Bond Market Is Screaming. The Stock Market Can't Hear It.
highlights: Bond volatility just jumped 35% in a month, junk bond spreads are starting to widen, and the VIX is asleep at 15. Credit has called every major stock top since 2007, and it's flashing again. Oct 05, 2026 The stock market’s fear gauge, the VIX, closed Friday at 15.31, near its lowest levels of the year. The bond market’s fear gauge, the MOVE Index, closed the same day at 107.29 after jumping roughly 35% in September. When those two indices disagree this badly, the bond market has usually been right first, and as of last week, credit spreads have started siding with bonds. If you don’t understand the credit markets, you do not understand the stock markets. The third signal in this report is the credit spread, which is the extra yield that weaker companies must pay above Treasuries to borrow money. When spreads widen, lenders are demanding more pay for the risk of not getting their money back. The MOVE Index rose 35% in September through September 28, a monthly jump seen only 8 times since 2008. During the week of September 25 alone, it climbed about 30%, its biggest weekly gain since the April 2025 tariff shock. Credit is the second domino, and it has started to tip (still very early). The intermarket chain runs in order: bond volatility rises first, credit spreads widen second, and stocks crack last. Chart 4 shows that order from January 2006 to October 2026. In 2007, the junk bond spread bottomed and started rising months before the S&P 500 peaked in October 2007. In mid-2014, spreads turned higher roughly a year before the S&P 500 topped in May 2015 and fell into its August 2015 and early 2016 selloffs. In the second half of 2021, spreads bottomed again ahead of the January 2022 stock peak. Lenders spotted the stress first every time, because bondholders only care about getting repaid and watch balance sheets more closely than stock buyers do. The high-yield (junk bond) spread widened from 2.93% on September 25 to 3.24% on October 1, a 31 basis point jump in 4 trading days. Chart 5’s top panel shows the all-in yield on junk bonds at 8.22% as of October 1, 2026, breaking above its 12-month average of 7.08%. Companies with weaker balance sheets now pay more than 8% to borrow, and the ones facing large debt maturities in 2026 and 2027 must refinance at those rates or default. Rising rates on revolving credit can have a big negative impact on businesses that don’t make any money or have very small margins. The bottom panel is the price ratio. It divides TLT by HYG (a junk bond ETF) to compare duration risk with credit risk. The ratio has fallen from about 2.5 in 2020 to 1.01 today, meaning investors spent 6 years preferring junk bonds over long Treasuries, a trade that works only while spreads stay tight. Spreads are still well below the long-term average of 5.17%, so they have plenty of room to widen, and a rising MOVE is what historically pushes them there. A Fed pause does nothing for long-term yields, which climbed without any help from the Fed and ignored Friday’s jobs data entirely. Tight spreads are a starting point with no cushion, which means a widening cycle has further to run. And the strong market is narrow. The S&P 500 is up 12.81% this year, but the equal-weight version is up only 9.47% through October 2, and in September roughly 3/4 of S&P 500 stocks fell while 4 stocks delivered about half the index’s 2026 gain. A low VIX on top of a handful of chipmakers is a crowded trade that breaks hard when rates move. Do not chase an 8% junk bond yield. At a 3.24% spread, you are paid very little extra for lending to the weakest companies right as their borrowing costs jump. Watch two levels. If the MOVE breaks above its March 2026 high near 115 and the junk spread climbs above 4%, rate stress will have reached corporate balance sheets, and the VIX at 15 will not survive it. The next tests are the Fed decision on October 28, 2026 and Treasury’s quarterly refunding announcement in early November, which tells the market how much more long-term debt is coming. If supply keeps climbing, mortgage rates and corporate refinancing costs go higher, and stocks will be the last asset to reprice.

[ ](https://cryptoslate.com/author/liam-akiba-wright/) By [Liam 'Akiba' Wright](https://cryptoslate.com/author/liam-akiba-wright/) Editor-in-Chief • CryptoSlate Oct. 5, 2026 ** 2 min read **## Quick Take 1. 01 US credit spreads widened from September 25 to October 1, with the largest increase in the weakest-rated debt. 2. 02 Investment-grade widening shows pressure beyond the weakest borrowers, while overlapping high-yield indices limit claims about its breadth. 3. 03 Whether credit repricing pressures Bitcoin depends on financing costs, institutional risk-taking and demand. The largest increase remained concentrated in CCC-and-lower debt, while investment-grade bonds showed a much smaller rise. results.title: iFlow | Investor Trends | Higher Treasury yields haven’t dented IG credit
highlights: Higher Treasury yields haven’t dented IG credit **Investor Trends** provides a deep dive into patterns and behaviors in equity, bond and currency markets around globe, underpinned with deeper macro insights. David Tam October 09, 2026 **JUMP TO** Tight spreads despite rising yields Key Highlights * IG spreads hold near post-2008 lows * Investors reallocate within fixed income, not out of it * Benchmark Treasury weights limit rotation out of IG **Seeming disconnect:** Treasury yields have risen to their highest levels in decades. Normally, higher risk-free rates driven by the market pricing a more hawkish Fed might pressure credit spreads to widen through two main transmission mechanisms: But IG spreads have remained very well contained. Exhibit 1 shows a scatterplot of daily observations of 10y yields and IG spreads since 2008. The orange dot in the bottom right represents the 10y treasury yield and IG credit OAS level on October 8. Even as yields have risen in recent months to their highest levels in decades, IG credit OAS is only 9bp off its post-2008 low. **Outflows from IG:** Over Q3, investor sentiment turned negative toward IG credit with selling picking up in September before starting to recover in October (Exhibit 2). iFlow data show that IG credit saw negative scored flows, signifying outflows, for eight consecutive weeks through early October, with selling easing in the latest reading. Over the same time frame, the spreads on the Bloomberg aggregate corporate IG index widened by only 3bp, suggesting that while the outflow streak was persistent, it was fairly orderly. Further, the market seemed to grow more discerning with IG credit spreads staying well contained while high-yield spreads widened by as many as 54bp before narrowing over the past week. **Modest inflows into Treasurys: **By contrast, Exhibit 2 also shows that Treasurys have enjoyed consistent though modest inflows throughout the quarter, with only two weeks of outflows since the end of June. Far from suggesting an aversion to Treasurys, the rising yield environment has provided investors an opportunity to tactically add to positions at a more attractive entry point. **Support for Treasurys: **If Treasury yields continue to rise while IG spreads hold, we should expect a marginal additional incentive to rotate out of IG and into Treasurys. Over time, this should be supportive of Treasurys and might lead IG credit spreads to widen. **Limits to the rotation: **Investors may care less about whether spreads are tight in historical percentile terms if the outright yield exceeds return targets. This is particularly true if they feel as if a recession or credit deterioration aren’t imminent, in which case investors may be happy to accept tight spreads to capture the incremental income. **Fixed income as a growing pie: **All-in yields across fixed income are growing more attractive as they’re generally priced off of a Treasury base that’s rising (Exhibit 4). This should entice inflows into multiple fixed income asset classes at once, as cash on the sidelines hunts for yield and equity investors concerned with stretched valuations seek out safety. Treasurys growing more appealing needn’t come at the expense of IG, as new money enters fixed income and spreads can remain tight if the asset class as a whole grows more appealing. * Track weekly scored flows into IG credit, Treasurys (Exhibit 2) and other fixed income asset classes to test whether investors are continuing to reallocate within fixed income and whether fixed income in general is seeing inflows. Persistent Treasury inflows alongside orderly IG outflows only would support the thesis that all-in yields are expanding the fixed income opportunity set rather than forcing a wholesale rotation out of credit. * Monitor the joint path of IG spreads, Treasury yields (Exhibits 1 and 4) and IG all-in yields to see whether higher risk-free rates continue to coexist with relatively contained spreads. If Treasury yields rise further while spreads remain near recent tights, it would reinforce the idea that investors are prioritizing outright yield and that tight spreads can coexist with high Treasury yields.

results.title: Corporate Bonds - Investment Grade & High Yield
highlights: Corporate & High Yield Bond Yields and Spreads | About This Page This page provides an overview of U.S. Investment Grade Corporate Bond and High Yield Bond yields, including currrent yields along with historical yield movements and spread analysis. For additional notes and data sources, continue reading below or click the info button at the top right of any chart. This chart shows the market yields for corporate bonds, for both investment grade and high yield bonds. The yields are based on the yields of a broad basket of bonds in the respective categories. The 10-year Treasury yield is also included as a reference benchmark. The riskiness of corporate bonds is measured by their credit ratings, which categorize bonds into two broad types: investment grade and high yield (or junk bonds). Ratings agencies like Moody's, Standard & Poor's, and Fitch assign these ratings based on the financial health and stability of the issuer. In the S&P system, the best companies receive ratings of AAA, and ratings of AA, A, and BBB are all considered high quality. BB, B, CCC, CC, C, D, and worse are lower quality bonds, but can offer a higher return for investors willing to take on higher risk. - Investment Grade Bonds: These are issued by companies with higher credit ratings (BBB and above), indicating a lower risk of default. Investment-grade bonds are considered relatively safe investments and, therefore, typically offer only slightly higher yields than Treasury bonds. The yields on the bonds of the strongest companies, such as Apple and Microsoft, are typically less than 1% higher since investors feel there is little risk that the companies will default on their loans. - High Yield Bonds: Also known colloquially as junk bonds, these bonds come from companies with lower credit ratings (BB or worse), suggesting a higher risk of default. Consequently, they offer higher yields to attract investors willing to accept the increased risk. While the term "junk bonds" may sound like these are some dodgy companies, the bonds of many well known large companies fall in this category. Companies such as American Airlines, Caesars Entertainment, Walgreens, DirecTV, and many other well known brands have had bonds in this category. Depending on the quality of the company and the terms of the bond, the spread (or extra yield demanded by investors) compared to Treasuries for high yield bonds can range from less than 3% to over 15%. The Current Yields chart shows the current yields for investment grade and high yield corporate bonds for varying ratings within each category. Corporate Bond Spreads This chart shows the spreads for corporate bonds, for both investment grade and high yield bonds. The spread is the difference in yield between the respective corporate bonds and Treasuries of similar maturity. Refer to the info pane on the Yields chart for more details on corporate bond types and ratings. Spreads as a Signal Through the magnitude of spreads compared to risk-free Treasuries, corporate bonds also offer a great barometer on the health of the economy. When corporate and high yield bond spreads are low, it signals optimism in the economy and low fears about corporate defaults and bankruptcies. In times of economic stress, the spreads become much higher, signaling the market's fear that many companies may be at risk of default.

results.title: Credit Spreads Explained: Investment Grade vs High Yield and What Widening Signals | Referently.com
highlights: October 6, 2026 A credit spread is the extra yield a company pays to borrow compared with the US government for the same length of time. If a five-year Treasury yields 4 percent and a company’s five-year bond yields 5.5 percent, the spread is 1.5 percentage points, or 150 basis points (one basis point is 0.01 point). That gap is the market’s price for the chance the company won’t pay back, plus a bit for being harder to sell than a Treasury. Spreads move every day, and they move before most other signs of trouble. When companies get into difficulty, bond investors usually notice first, and that makes spreads one of the best real-time stress gauges in finance. - ICE BofA US Corporate Index OAS covers investment-grade bonds (rated BBB- or higher) with at least $250 million outstanding and more than a year to maturity. - ICE BofA US High Yield Index OAS covers bonds rated below investment grade, often called junk. Investment grade vs high yield The split follows the credit rating scale. Bonds rated BBB- or Baa3 and above are investment grade (IG); anything lower is high yield (HY). Our guide to credit rating scales shows how S&P, Moody’s and Fitch line up and how default rates jump below the cutoff. That jump is why the two markets behave like different asset classes. | | Investment grade | High yield | | --- | --- | --- | | Ratings | AAA to BBB- | BB+ and below | | Typical issuers | Apple, utilities, big banks, hyperscalers | Private-equity-owned companies, smaller cable, energy and retail firms | | What drives the spread | Interest rates, supply, broad risk appetite | Default risk, recovery values, the economy | | Long-run average OAS (1997 to 2025) | About 1.9 points (median about 1.7) | About 5.2 points (median about 4.6) | | “Normal” range | Roughly 1.0 to 2.5 points | Roughly 3 to 8 points | | Early October 2026 | About 0.85 points | About 3.1 points | About half of the IG market by value is now rated BBB, the lowest rung, compared with about a quarter in the late 1990s. That matters in a downturn. A BBB company cut to BB becomes a “fallen angel”, and many insurance companies and IG-only funds have to sell it, so a wave of downgrades can push big volumes of debt into a high-yield market that has trouble absorbing it. Spreads spend long stretches tight and then gap wider in hurry. These are the landmark readings on ICE BofA indexes: | Episode | High-yield OAS | Investment-grade context | | --- | --- | --- | | Mid-2007, pre-crisis low | About 2.4 points, the tightest on record | Very tight | | Mid-December 2008, after Lehman | Roughly 20 points, the widest on record | BBB spreads above 6 points | | 2015 to 2016 oil crash | About 8.9 points | Moderate widening | | March 23, 2020, Covid shock | 10.87 points | BBB spreads around 4 points or more | | April 7, 2025, tariff shock | 4.61 points | IG at 1.20 points | | 2026 lows | 2.60 points (August 28) | IG at 0.73 points (January) | Two things stand out In 2008 spreads stayed above 10 for months, because defaults were real and the banking system was . In 2020 they more than doubled in about a and then gave back a large part of move within weeks, buy corporate bonds, a first. always the deepest one. it doesn’ A wider spread means want more compensation to lend to companies. The reasons differ, and widening tells you which one is in play - HY widens a lot, IG barely moves. The market is worried about weak borrowers specifically: default risk, refinancing walls, a sector in trouble. This is the classic early-slowdown pattern. - Both widen together, sharply. A broad risk-off move or a liquidity squeeze, often alongside a spike in the VIX. Funds sell what they can, not what they want to. - CCC widens while BB holds. Trouble is concentrated in the weakest tier. Those names usually default first. - IG widens on heavy issuance. Supply alone can push spreads out when big borrowers flood the market, which says less about credit quality. Spreads have tended to widen before and during recessions, and HY spreads above roughly 5 to 6 points have historically lined up with recessionary conditions. They are a better confirming signal than a long-range forecaster. They compare well with the yield curve, which gives early but unreliable warnings; spreads give later warnings that are rarely false. Very tight spreads have their own message: lenders are being paid little for the risk they take, so there’s not much cushion if things go wrong. Late-cycle tights, such as mid-2007, have come before some of the worst periods for credit. Equity sentiment gauges like the CNN Fear & Greed Index include a junk bond demand component for this reason. Where things stand in October 2026 After a long squeeze lower, spreads have started to move. The high-yield OAS touched 2.60 points on August 28, 2026, among the tightest readings since 2007. By October 1 it was 3.24 points before easing to 3.10, a widening of more than half a point in about a month. Investment-grade spreads, which were as tight as 0.73 points in January 2026, have drifted out to about 0.85. The causes being cited are mostly about supply and rates, not defaults. September brought heavy junk issuance, and investors are digesting huge borrowing tied to AI data centers, with hyperscalers increasingly funding capex through bond sales. The pressure has been sharpest in the lowest-rated bonds. Higher Treasury yields add to it: the 10-year is above 5 percent and the Fed raised rates in September 2026, which lifts the all-in cost of borrowing even where spreads hold. This page reflects conditions as of early October 2026. - HY OAS level and speed. A move from 3 to 4 points in a few weeks matters more than a slow drift. Above 5 to 6 points, markets are pricing a real slowdown. - The HY minus IG gap. A widening gap means the market is separating weak borrowers from strong ones. For definitions of the terms used here, the Referently glossary of financial markets covers OAS, basis points and the rest. The practical rule: a slow drift in spreads is mostly noise about supply and rates. A fast move in high yield, led by the weakest borrowers and not reversed within weeks, is the credit market telling you something the stock market may not have priced yet.

results.title: High Yield Corporate Bond Spread Today: 3.15% (Oct 2026)
highlights: High Yield Corporate Bond Spread Today: 3.15% (Oct 2026) | MacroRadar A US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread. Updated 2026-10-08 · daily→ Stable High yield spread — latest reading: 3.15 percent. As of October 2026, it is up 17.5% over the past 12 months, above its 10-year average. Source: BAMLH0A0HYM2, ICE Data Indices, published daily. Reported as published, without transformation; the publisher may revise it. The financial-conditions regime is currently neutral (97% confidence). The high‑yield spread sitting at 3.15% is modestly above average and has held steady with a small rise, suggesting investors are tolerating a moderate level of credit risk. Its 62nd percentile shows it’s higher than most recent readings, pointing to a slightly tighter risk appetite. The high-yield spread is the extra yield, measured in percentage points, that investors demand to hold below-investment-grade corporate bonds — 'junk' bonds — instead of safe Treasuries of similar maturity. The non-obvious refinement is that this is an option-adjusted spread, or OAS, which strips out the effect of the call and prepayment options embedded in many corporate bonds so that what remains is a cleaner read on pure credit risk. It answers a single question with unusual clarity: how worried is the bond market about corporate defaults right now? Because high-yield issuers are the corner of the corporate credit market, the spread on their debt is the canary in the coal mine grow confident, thin compensation for spread narrows; In calm, confident markets the spread typically sits somewhere around 3 to 5 percentage points — the ordinary premium for owning riskier corporate debt. As conditions tighten, it climbs through the mid-single digits into territory that signals real concern, and in a full-blown crisis it can blow out into the high teens or beyond. The late-2008 panic drove the spread past roughly 20 percentage points, an extraordinary level implying the market expected a wave of defaults; the March 2020 COVID shock pushed it to around 10 percentage points in a matter of weeks. The dominant drivers are the perceived probability of corporate defaults and the market's appetite for risk. When the economy is strong and financing is easy, default expectations fall and investors reach for yield, compressing the spread. When growth slows, earnings weaken, or funding markets seize up, default fears rise and the spread widens — often sharply, because the marginal buyer of junk debt can vanish quickly when sentiment turns. Liquidity matters too: in a panic, the difficulty of selling lower-quality bonds at all adds a liquidity premium on top of pure credit risk. Monetary policy and broad financial conditions sit behind all of this. Aggressive rate hikes and a shrinking pool of liquidity raise refinancing costs for indebted companies and tend to widen spreads, while rate cuts and ample liquidity ease the pressure. Oil and commodity shocks can also move the index disproportionately, because energy and resource companies have at times made up a large share of the high-yield universe, so a collapse in oil prices can drag the whole spread wider even when the rest of the economy is steady. The series is the ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread, published by ICE Data Indices and sourced here from FRED as BAMLH0A0HYM2, updated every business day. It is computed by taking a broad index of US dollar-denominated below-investment-grade corporate bonds, calculating the spread of each bond's yield over the Treasury curve, applying an option-adjustment to remove the distortions from embedded call and prepayment features, and aggregating across the index. The result is a single percentage-point figure representing the market-wide credit-risk premium on junk debt. The high-yield spread is the most volatile member of the risk complex it shares with the VIX Volatility Index and the Baa Corporate Bond Spread. The Baa spread covers the lowest tier of investment-grade debt and is the more conservative, slower-moving credit gauge, while this high-yield measure captures the riskiest borrowers and moves first and farthest. Reading the two credit spreads together shows how far stress has traveled up the quality ladder — junk-only stress versus stress that has reached investment-grade names is a meaningful distinction. Against the VIX, the high-yield spread offers a cross-check between the bond and equity markets' read on risk. When both blow out together, the market is pricing a fundamental deterioration; when the spread widens while equity volatility stays calm, credit may be flashing an early warning that stocks have not yet acknowledged. Pairing the spread with the Federal Funds Rate and the Crude Oil Price helps explain whether tightening policy or an energy shock is doing the widening. The macro-regime panel above frames the current reading. A spread sitting in the calm 3-to-5-point band against a healthy growth backdrop describes a market comfortable with corporate credit risk and easy financing conditions, while a spread climbing through the mid-single digits and beyond reflects rising default fears that have historically accompanied tightening conditions or economic stress. The trajectory often matters more than the level — a spread quietly widening from a low base can be more informative than a high but stable one. For long-term investors, the high-yield spread is one of the clearest windows into the health of the credit cycle, which underpins the broader economy. Because it has historically widened ahead of and during downturns, it offers an early read on whether financial conditions are loosening or tightening — information that bears on everything from corporate refinancing risk to the durability of an expansion. It also helps frame the reward for taking credit risk: a thin spread means investors are being paid little to own fragile debt. The high yield spread measures the difference between yields on high yield (junk) corporate bonds and Treasury bonds of similar maturity. A wider spread means investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk — a sign of stress or pessimism. Widening spreads often precede economic downturns — they signal that investors are worried about corporate defaults. Tight spreads indicate confidence and easy financial conditions. Credit spreads are one of the most reliable forward-looking stress indicators.

results.title: Goldman: Treasury Yields Now Drive Most of a Corporate Bond's Return | Previct.ai
highlights: With credit spreads contributing under 15% of investment-grade yield, Goldman Sachs argues corporate bonds increasingly trade as a rates product — a shift that changes what buyers are actually being paid for. - Goldman Sachs says investment-grade credit spreads now make up under 15% of all-in yield, versus roughly 45% on average in 2019-2021. - In high yield, spreads contribute about 37% of yield, down from roughly 75% previously. - Higher sovereign yields let pensions, insurers and foreign investors hit all-in yield targets despite tight spreads, making corporate bonds behave more like a rates product. Elevated U.S. Treasury yields have made corporate credit attractive even at historically tight spreads, because the risk-free component now supplies the bulk of the return, Goldman Sachs said. In U.S. investment-grade credit, spreads account for less than 15% of total yield, down from roughly 45% on average between 2019 and 2021. In high yield, spreads contribute about 37% of all-in yield, versus roughly 75% previously. The practical consequence is that a larger share of corporate bond performance now tracks the direction of government yields rather than the creditworthiness of issuers. Goldman's figures put the spread contribution below 15% of investment-grade yield and around 37% in high yield, against roughly 45% and about 75% respectively in 2019-2021. In that environment, a portfolio of corporate credit behaves more like a quasi-rates product: duration and rate expectations matter more, and the credit spread offers less cushion if default risk rises. The transmission channel runs through the risk-free component: with spreads supplying a small share of all-in yield, corporate credit is more sensitive to moves in government yields and less cushioned by credit spread. That cuts both ways — falling yields would lift these bonds, while rising yields would pressure them, and a widening of spreads would matter less in total-return terms than the same spread move did in 2019-2021.

results.title: Stock Losses Deepen on AI Trade, Treasuries Rally: Markets Wrap - SWI swissinfo.ch
highlights: (Bloomberg) — Global stock losses deepened as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade pushed investors out of one of the market’s hottest corners this year. Treasuries rallied on haven demand. MSCI Inc.’s Asia Pacific equities gauge dropped 1.6%, set for its lowest close since August. The Kospi Index in South Korea — a key barometer of the AI trade — tumbled 6% as concerns over Chinese competition spurred investors to rotate out of the tech sector. SK Hynix Inc. sank 10% and Samsung Electronics Co. about 8%. US and European equity-index futures also retreated, pointing to further pressure on global shares. The losses in Asia followed a Wall Street selloff that left the Nasdaq 100 Index at this month’s low and a US gauge of chip stocks at its weakest since mid-September. Declines in stocks and falling oil prices lifted bonds and European bond futures. The yield on the benchmark Treasury 10-year note fell four basis points to 5.20% as cash trading resumed after a holiday. Brent crude dropped 0.9% to about $105.70 a barrel. Meanwhile, a Bloomberg gauge of the dollar edged lower, snapping a four-day gain. The stock selloff drove investors toward bonds, lifting Treasuries across the curve. Government debt in Australia and New Zealand also advanced. results.title: Dollar slips from 18-month high as oil prices fall, inflation data in focus | live
highlights: NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The dollar slipped from an 18-month high on Tuesday as oil prices retreated and investors reassessed the AI-fueled rally that has supported demand for US assets this year, while awaiting fresh clues on the Federal Reserve's interest rate path. Oil prices fell 0.86% to $105.75 per barrel on Tuesday, as traders weighed the prospect of additional Russian diesel supplies. Russia said it can restore diesel exports beyond levels Trump outlined in a deal with Moscow. "The dollar (is) a little weaker on slightly lower oil. Large bank earnings this morning were mixed, shedding little light on the broader equity outlook," said John Velis, Americas macro strategist at BNY. "With bond yields slightly off recent highs, the dollar looks to trade slightly softer on the day." The US dollar index, a measure of the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, slid 0.25% to 102.27 after reaching 102.61 on Monday, its highest level since April 2025. Investors are now awaiting the release on Wednesday of the US Consumer Price Index for September, which should provide further clues about possible Fed policy tightening. Traders see about an 80% chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, up from 51% a month ago, while pricing in about 75 basis points of tightening by late 2027, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. Investors abandoned bets on a Fed rate hike later this month after two policymakers argued for gathering more evidence before deciding whether further tightening is needed, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller said inflation expectations remained "well anchored." Rising oil prices recently have been supporting the dollar at the expense of currencies such as the euro and yen, which are linked to economies far more dependent than the US on imported oil. The euro rebounded from a roughly 17-month low on Tuesday despite another jump in gas prices, a key driver of euro zone inflation, while concerns over France's fiscal outlook persisted. It was up 0.3% at $1.1189 after hitting $1.11525 on Monday, its lowest level since May 2025. The yen strengthened 0.15% to 158.38 against the dollar after Bank of Japan data showed wholesale prices rose 6.8% in the year to September, missing a median market forecast of 7.6% but still enough to justify market fears of higher interest rates. of official intervention excessive currency moves The euro was last up 0.21% at 177.32 versus the Japanese currency, after hitting 176.25, its lowest level since November 2025. The Australian dollar was at $0.6979, following the release of the minutes from the Reserve Bank of Australia's September board meeting. The board voted unanimously to raise rates for the fourth time this year.

results.title: AI Doubts and Heavier Fuel Charges Send Stocks South for Second Consecutive Day: Oct. 13, 2026
highlights: Charges Send Stocks South for Stocks are sinking for the second consecutive session as doubts concerning AI’s ability to power corporate earnings much further coincide with heavier fuel charges that are supporting lofty Treasury yields. Investors are indeed worried about the possibility for profit deceleration alongside restrictive financial conditions, as elevated interest rates could start to bite in the coming months. Ongoing Middle East violence that is bolstering crude prices, meanwhile, is blocking potential gains for the cyclically oriented parts of the market, which have previously dampened adverse impacts upon broad indices when the tech trade has buckled, like it is today. As a result of the weaker risk sentiment and increasingly challenging macroeconomic backdrop, 9 of the 11 US principal sectors are retreating as well as the four major equity benchmarks. This morning’s economic calendar, furthermore, failed to rally the bulls, as decreasing small-business optimism that missed expectations, rising existing-home sales that beat projections, and fast hiring from the weekly ADP-employment survey essentially fell on deaf ears, although it helped raise the short-end of the curve via strengthening labor momentum that widened the path for a Fed hike or two. Separately, the longer-dated tenors have been catching safe-haven bids resulting, in part, from a modest uptick in slowdown angst that is additionally weighing on the greenback. Elsewhere, cryptocurrencies are rallying, non-energy commodities are sliding, volatility protection instruments are reflecting heightening hedging demand and prediction markets are experiencing engagement. With corporate earnings growth in the nosebleeds amidst expectations for decelerating profit expansions in the coming quarters, investors want to feel optimistic about 2027 prior to adding meaningful exposure. The current slowdown anxiety paired with lofty interest rates is the primary reason, in my view, that stocks have been relatively flat in the past ten weeks, as we continue to trade at the same levels as in early August. Meanwhile, tomorrow’s Consumer Price Index alongside incoming quarterly reports will provide evidence of the temperature of inflation as well as the buoyancy of revenues, incomes and margins, which together may signal favorable comps for cost pressures as we turn the calendar amidst disadvantageous reference points for bottom lines. Wall Street could digest an environment of weaker payouts and still post gains against the backdrop of looser financial conditions stemming from the Fed’s 2% objective being easier to get to in consideration of the average West Texas Intermediate charge in 2026 standing at around $87 per barrel. The anemic sales have occurred as the UK is working on its next budget. While the country is seeking to increase defense spending and maintain spending on health care, doing so could require an additional £35 billion without cutting other items from the budget, according to a recent study from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. With soaring interests resulting from growing government deficits, AI companies issuing debt and intensifying inflations fears triggered by the US-Iran war, the UK is facing mounting pressure to show that it can get its finances under control. Chancellor John Healey is scheduled to release his spending plans on Oct. 28. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 300 points, or 0.6% as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, while the Nasdaq composite was 0.4% lower. results.title: BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral and buys Treasuries as 10-year yield nears 5.25%
highlights: BlackRock cuts US stocks to neutral and buys Treasuries as 10-year yield nears 5.25% - BlackRock cut US equities to neutral from overweight in a short-term risk-management move and upgraded short-dated Treasuries to overweight, saying markets have overpriced 160bp of Fed tightening as 10-year yields climbed to around 5.25% this year. BlackRock’s shift adds weight to the case that higher yields are starting to compete with equities for capital, a dynamic that could cap stock valuations even as earnings stay strong. The key swing factor is oil: Middle East war and higher crude prices have driven the sharp repricing of Fed expectations, so any easing in the Iran war would support BlackRock’s view that rate-hike bets are overdone and favour its short-end Treasury call. Conversely, a further oil spike that lifts this week’s CPI and PPI could push yields higher still and test the cushion BlackRock estimates before Treasury returns turn negative. Demand from large allocators at these yields may also help steady the long end after recent volatility, while the trimmed JGB underweight suggests Japanese yields above 3% are drawing more interest. - BlackRock closed its long-held overweight on US equities, moving to neutral, describing it as a short-term risk-management step in a volatile macro and market environment - The firm said its core convictions on AI transformation remain intact, and it still favours AI-related companies, listed infrastructure and emerging market equities - It upgraded shorter-term Treasuries to overweight and long-term Treasuries to neutral, ending an underweight held for most of the past six years - BlackRock said the 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening priced in since January is overdone, with the 10-year yield up 110 basis points this year to around 5.25% - It estimates a cushion of about 75 basis points against further yield rises over 12 months before Treasury total returns turn negative - The firm also trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds and cut US agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral to help fund the shift BlackRock has closed its long-held overweight position in US equities, moving to neutral as part of a shift that sees the world’s largest asset manager adding US Treasuries after rising yields made government bonds more attractive. The firm described the equity downgrade as a short-term risk-management move rather than a change in its core views, saying investors need to be more dynamic in today’s volatile macro and market regime. It said it is also watching growing public attention to AI policy and to the build-out of AI infrastructure across US jurisdictions. BlackRock said its convictions on AI transformation remain intact. It argued that higher rates are increasingly separating companies that can generate returns above their cost of capital from those that cannot, and it continues to favour AI-related companies and listed infrastructure, where strong demand and scarcity support returns. It also kept its overweight on emerging market equities. The move comes even as third-quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are expected to grow nearly 30% from a year earlier, according to FactSet data cited in the note. Proceeds from taking profits on US stocks are partly funding a significant upgrade to Treasuries. BlackRock said the 10-year Treasury yield has risen 110 basis points this year to around 5.25%, driven mainly by higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations or term premium, the extra return investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds. It attributed the rise in real rates to intensifying competition for capital, which is pushing up the neutral rate, and to a sharp reversal in Fed expectations driven by Middle East tensions and higher oil prices. Markets have priced in 160 basis points of additional Fed tightening over the next 12 months since January, which BlackRock considers overdone. The firm upgraded shorter-term Treasuries to overweight, where it sees the most scope for tightening expectations to unwind, and long-term Treasuries to neutral, saying higher yields now better compensate investors for interest rate risk. BlackRock said it had been underweight Treasuries for most of the past six years, first moving there in October 2020 when 10-year yields were near 0.9%. At current levels, it estimates yields could rise a further 75 basis points over 12 months before total returns turn negative. In other changes, BlackRock trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds, a position held since July 2023 when 10-year yields were around 0.4% to 0.5%, compared with above 3% now. It also cut US agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral. The firm said it stands ready to add risk again as visibility improves. This week’s US CPI and PPI reports, the first snapshots of September inflation, are likely to shape Fed rate expectations and Treasury yields. Why its calls matter: when a manager this size shifts its views, as it did today by cutting US stocks to neutral and adding Treasuries, the change can steer flows across its model portfolios and is closely watched by other investors as a signal of institutional sentiment.
