highlights: Chip Stocks Get Crushed as Korea's KOSPI Drops 5%, J&J Falls 6%: Markets Today A memory-chip scare out of China hammered Samsung and SK Hynix in Seoul, spilled into Micron and Applied Materials, and dragged the Nasdaq lower, while big-bank earnings kept the Dow from falling apart. - Chip stocks sold off hard after China's CXMT announced progress on a more efficient memory-cell design, sending Samsung and SK Hynix down roughly 8% each in Seoul and dragging South Korea's KOSPI down 5%. - The pain spread to U.S. semiconductors: Micron dropped 4.9% and Applied Materials tumbled 6.5%, with the Nasdaq 100 leading index declines at -0.5%. - Big-bank earnings were a mixed bag: JPMorgan rose about 1% despite a profit miss, Goldman Sachs jumped on a huge beat, and Wells Fargo fell 1.5% on a revenue shortfall. - Johnson & Johnson sank 6.2% despite a profit beat and raised full-year outlook, weighed down by a MedTech miss and a one-time talc litigation charge. - Energy and communications held firm while industrials and health care slid, with WTI crude near $93.95 and the 10-year Treasury yield holding near 5.22%. U.S. stocks slipped by midday Tuesday, and the culprit was a chip-sector rout sparked by a 5% plunge in South Korea's KOSPI. That was enough to offset gains in banks and energy, leaving the S&P 500 hovering just below 7,800 while the Nasdaq 100 led the declines. Here's the chain of events. China's CXMT announced progress on a more efficient memory-cell design, and that was all it took to send Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (OTC: SSNLF) and SK Hynix Inc. (NASDAQ: SKHY) down roughly 8% each in Seoul. Memory chips are a commodity business with brutal economics, and anything that smells like more efficient supply tends to make existing producers nervous. That spilled straight into U.S. semiconductors, where Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ: MU) dropped 4.9% and Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT) tumbled 6.5%. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2% to 7,795. The Nasdaq 100 fell 0.5% to 30,511, with chip weakness weighing on it. The Russell 2000 lost 0.6% to 2,777. Banks did their part to hold things together. JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM) rose about 1% even after its profit of $15.3 billion, or $5.57 per share, missed the $5.90 estimate. Meanwhile Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE: GS) gained after earnings of $17.01 per share crushed the $13.02 consensus. That's not a beat, that's a different sport. Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE: WFC) fell 1.5% even as earnings of $1.87 per share topped the $1.84 consensus, because revenue of $21.87 billion missed the $22.31 billion forecast. Profits are nice, but the top line is where the story lives. Elsewhere among blue-chip stocks, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) sank 6.2% despite a profit beat and a raised full-year outlook, weighed by a MedTech miss and a one-time talc litigation charge. Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE: CAT) fell 5.0% in the broader industrials pullback. In energy, WTI crude traded near $93.95 per barrel, up 0.2%, while Brent edged 0.9% lower to $105.72. Gasoline has now tied 2022's record for most days above $4 per gallon in a single year. That's the kind of stat that shows up in grocery-aisle conversations. results.title: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 7,798, Nasdaq 27,200, Dow 51,837 as MU Slides 4.45%
highlights: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 7,798, Nasdaq 27,200, Dow 51,837 as MU Slides 4.45% * Micron MU fell 4.45% to $945.03, erasing $50 billion in value on China’s CXMT DRAM breakthrough. * JPMorgan JPM earned $5.57 a share on $50.2 billion in revenue, 33 cents short of the $5.90 consensus. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened Tuesday, October 13, 2026, like a market that had found its catalyst. Dow futures traded at 52,580, up 470 points or 0.90%, ten minutes before the bell, and the cash index printed 52,245.14 shortly after the open, a gain of 394.59 points or 0.76% on Monday’s close of 51,850.55. By 10:30 a.m. ET the index sat at 51,837.83, down 12.72 points or 0.02%. Roughly 407 points of upside, gone in under an hour, on a morning when the earnings news was mostly good. The S&P 500 never had the lift. It opened down 0.07% and was trading at 7,798.11 by mid-morning, off 9.13 points or 0.12%, leaving it 46.56 points, or 0.6%, below its all-time high of 7,844.67 set earlier this month. The Nasdaq Composite opened down 0.31% and was quoted at 27,200.61, a 0.17% decline that is smaller than the 0.36% hole it opened in. The Russell 2000 sat at 2,782.21, down 12.27 points or 0.44%, extending Monday’s 0.45% drop. That combination is the session’s real signal. Banks and health care delivered a cluster of beats and raised forecasts before 8 a.m., and the price-weighted Dow pulled 400 points of value out of them on the opening bell. Then the bid faded. The memory-chip liquidation that started in Seoul overnight kept compounding, and the Nasdaq actually stabilized while the Dow surrendered its gains, which tells you buyers were rotating out of the earnings winners rather than into them. in Asia. South Korea’s KOSPI fell 5.5% to 6% depending on the print, with Samsung Electronics down 7.39% and SK Hynix down roughly 8% in Seoul, extending both stocks’ losing streaks to five sessions. Those two companies account for more than half of the South Korean market’s total capitalization, so a The trigger is a design announcement out of China. ChangXin Memory Technologies, the Shanghai-listed DRAM maker known as CXMT, said over the weekend through its president Cao Kanyu that it has made progress on a 4F² DRAM cell structure, an architecture engineered to pack more storage into less silicon area. CXMT plans to introduce a server memory product built on that design by the end of 2026. CXMT’s own shares fell 2.79% in Shanghai, which says the market sees this as a threat to incumbents more than a windfall for the challenger. Micron Technology was one of the heaviest single weights on the S&P 500 Tuesday morning. The stock traded at $945.03 by 10:30 a.m. ET, down $44.01 or 4.45%, after trading as low as 5.8% lower in the first minutes of the session. At a $1.069 trillion market capitalization, the drop erased $50 billion in value before 11 a.m. Volume hit 10.02 million shares in the first hour against a three-month daily average of 32.3 million, a pace that projects well above normal turnover. Storage got hit harder than memory. Western Digital tumbled 7.71% in premarket trading after a price-target cut to $470 from $525. Seagate Technology sank 7.28% on the broader storage selloff, with reports of a multibillion-dollar acquisition bidding war and intensifying global competition in the mix. SanDisk fell between 6% and 7% in premarket, after dropping 6% on Monday. Storage and memory trade as one cycle in this market, and the CXMT news hit the whole capacity-constrained chain at once. On the other side of the AI ledger, the morning brought a fresh macro warning. The IMF flagged an AI slowdown and spiking bond yields as looming risks to global markets. With the 10-year yield at 5.22%, the cost of capital for long-duration AI projects is the highest it has been in more than two decades, and a CEO publicly questioning investor discipline lands harder in that rate environment than it would have at 4%. JPMorgan Chase opened bank earnings season with the only clear miss among the majors. The largest U.S. bank reported third-quarter net income of $15.3 billion, or $5.57 per share, up 6% from a year earlier. The consensus sat at $5.90, so the print came in 33 cents short. Net revenue rose 8% to $50.2 billion from $46.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025. The miss has an asterisk. JPMorgan booked $658 million in pretax losses on investment securities, and excluding that item the bank earned $5.75 a share. That still leaves a 15-cent gap to consensus, so the adjustment narrows the miss without erasing it. Securities losses in a quarter where the Fed hiked in September and the 10-year pushed above 5.2% are the most predictable line item in the release. Banks holding fixed-rate bonds bought at lower yields are carrying unrealized losses, and JPMorgan chose to crystallize some of them. The stock reaction tells you how low the bar had become. JPMorgan shares rose 1.02% in premarket trading despite the miss. Options had priced an earnings move between 3.4% and 5.2% depending on the snapshot, so a 1% gain on a miss is a market that came in braced for worse. Bank stocks had a rough three months coming into the print: the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index fell 8.4% over that stretch while the S&P 500 gained more than 3%. Inflation and the bond selloff hit revenue expectations and pressured bond portfolios, and many banks are sitting on unrealized losses. The engine was equities trading. Goldman’s equities business posted revenue of $6.44 billion, up 72% from a year earlier. The drivers were the conditions the rest of the market hated: the Fed’s September rate hike, the spike in fuel costs tied to the Middle East conflict, and the chip-stock selloff all forced institutional investors to reshuffle portfolios aggressively. That reshuffling runs through prime brokerage and trading desks, and Goldman’s equity financing business, lending to clients so they can trade stocks, captured a large share of the flow. Fixed income, currencies and commodities was the soft spot. FICC revenue came in at $3.47 billion, down 1% from a year ago. Goldman’s FICC line has been volatile all year: it fell 10% in the first quarter when the rates business was hit by volatility from the Iran war, then surged 32% in the second quarter before slipping in the third. Investment banking was a clear beat relative to consensus, a sign that the deal pipeline is intact even after JPMorgan described a late-September slowdown. UnitedHealth Group was the single biggest contributor to the Dow’s early rip. The largest U.S. health insurer reported third-quarter revenue of $112.7 billion, earnings from operations of $6.6 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, with GAAP EPS at $4.56, according to its SEC filing. Cash flow from operations came in at $5.1 billion, 1.2 times net income. The guidance raise is the headline. UnitedHealth now expects full-year 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share and GAAP earnings of at least $19.50. After the second quarter, the company had guided to $19.50 to $20.00 adjusted, which itself was a large lift from the prior floor above $17.75. The new floor sits 50 cents above the old top of the range, a 2.5% raise on the high end. The number investors watch most is the medical care ratio, the share of premium revenue paid out in claims. It came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. That compares with 86.7% in the second quarter, which benefited from $860 million in favorable prior-period reserve development, and with 89.9% in the third quarter of 2025 when medical cost trends were running at historic highs. The company credited medical cost management, pricing discipline, benefit design changes and care delivery enhancements. The operating cost ratio fell to 12.8% from 13.5% a year earlier, a 70-basis-point improvement that reflects the push to modernize operations and strip administrative cost.

results.title: [Closing Market] KOSPI Clings to 6,000 Amid Foreigners' Heavy Selling - Businesskorea
highlights: Foreign Net Selling Near 4.5 Trillion Won Sends Benchmark Down Over 5% with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix Plunging Due to Memory Competition Fears, Amid Won Weakening by 10 Won Against U.S. Dollar On Oct. 13, the domestic stock market faced a fierce selling offensive from foreign investors, staging a record-breaking plunge. As a massive volume of stocks flooded the market following the previous day, the KOSPI index instantly collapsed by more than 5%, facing a precarious market finale that threatened the 6,000 support level. The overall market appears to be severely frozen as anxiety surrounding global semiconductor industry conditions overlapped with the emergence of selling volume during the process of resolving the supply-demand concentration. On this day, the KOSPI index closed at 6,035.35, plummeting by 348.89 points (-5.46%) compared to the previous trading day. The index started at 6,186.08, slightly lower than the previous session, but expanded its losses as a bomb of selling volume from institutions and foreign investors poured in right after the opening. At one point during intraday trading, it was pushed back to the 5,911.11 level, temporarily breaking down the 6,000 level, but as some low-end buying entered near the market close, it barely recovered above the 6,030 level to finish the session. On this day, the KOSPI market capitalization was tallied at 4,986.333 trillion won (about $3.70 trillion). It fell below the 5,000 trillion won mark for the first time in about two and a half months since on July 30. The KOSDAQ index also failed to support its bottom and showed a bearish trend. The KOSDAQ closed at 837.03, down 1.43% from the previous trading day, fully inheriting the shockwave of the KOSPI market. It was a day when investment sentiment was extremely contracted as panic selling centered on large-cap stocks spread throughout small and medium-cap stocks. It is about 32% lower compared to this year’s intraday high for the KOSDAQ (1,229.42 on April 27). Foreign investors led the index decline by net selling trillions of won (approximately 4.5 trillion won or $3.34 billion) worth of stocks in the KOSPI market during this single day alone. The fierce emergence of foreign volume that has continued since late last week is analyzed to be caused by the increased valuation burden of the domestic stock market and global portfolio adjustments. On the news that Chinese memory semiconductor company ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) will release server semiconductors within the year, the stock prices of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix slid by 7.29% and 10.09%, respectively, on this day. Samsung Electronics closed with a significant drop compared to the previous trading day as it became the target of concentrated selling by foreigners and institutions. Amid the recent dilution of the safety net effect from treasury stock repurchases, the stock price was pushed back substantially, taking a direct hit from the aftermath of the global tech stock weakness. The drop in SK hynix was even steeper. SK hynix plummeted to the 1,489,000 won level at one point during intraday trading, and closed falling by 10.09% compared to the previous session . The controversy over the peak of memory semiconductors and concerns about the pursuit by Chinese competitors acted complexly, severely deteriorating investment sentiment. Won/Dollar Exchange Rate Rises by 10 Won in Line with Stock Market Plunge In the Seoul Foreign Exchange Market, the won-dollar exchange rate received upward pressure driven by the steep downward trend of the domestic stock market, foreign repatriation demand, and dollar futures buying. The won/dollar exchange rate rose by 10 won in a single day due to foreign dumping in the domestic stock market and macroeconomic bad news. Although the dollar buying volume from semiconductor export companies hit a yearly low during intraday trading, external risks eventually pulled up the upper limit. As of the close at 3:30 p.m. on this day, the won/dollar exchange rate recorded 1,345.1 won, rising by 10.0 won compared to the previous trading day. The won/dollar exchange rate fell to 1,331.2 won in the morning, breaking the yearly low for two consecutive days. This is interpreted as the result of continuous dollar buying demand from semiconductor export companies. The dollar showed strength as the preference for safe assets intensified in tandem with concerns about capital flight by stock market participants. However, the breakthrough of the 1,350 won line appeared to be blocked for now due to vigilance against smoothing operations by foreign exchange authorities. Nevertheless, it was insufficient to withstand the strong dollar pressure fueled by foreign net selling in the stock market, high oil prices, and high interest rates. The yen-won arbitrage exchange rate recorded 845.05 won per 100 yen, and the yuan-won exchange rate closed at 199.84 won, continuing the downward pressure on the won against neighboring currencies. In particular, the wait-and-see sentiment has reached its peak ahead of the announcement of the United States’ September Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the Monetary Policy Board, which will determine the direction of domestic monetary policy. In the short term, the futures trading patterns of foreigners and whether large-cap semiconductor stocks rebound are expected to be the key variables that will determine the safe settlement of the KOSPI 6,000 level. It is a time for market participants to focus on conservative risk management while checking the trends of external economic indicators rather than making unreasonable leverage investments.

results.title: Rising US Bond Yields Show No Sign of Slowing | SignalPro News
highlights: This year, an important psychological barrier for the bond market was crossed. Yields across different US Treasury maturities exceeded levels not seen in decades. And they show no sign of slowing down. (Source: Bloomberg) Rising US Treasury yields with no sign of slowing are likely to keep pressure on risk assets and support the US dollar, as higher discount rates compress equity valuations and tighten global financial conditions. The bond market's break above multi-decade yield barriers signals persistent term premium and fiscal supply concerns, which could trigger further repricing across rates and credit. Broad risk-off pressure on equities and credit, with the US dollar strengthening and gold and duration-sensitive assets facing headwinds. 1. 01 US Treasury yields across maturities have broken above psychological multi-decade barriers, signaling a structural shift in the rates regime. 2. 02 Higher yields raise the discount rate for equities, pressuring growth and tech stocks while steepening the curve and tightening financial conditions. 3. 03 The move shows no sign of slowing, implying continued upward pressure on global borrowing costs and potential stress in rate-sensitive sectors like real estate and emerging markets. Short-term · 0–24h Equity futures likely open lower, USD strengthens, and Treasury yields extend gains; gold and long-duration bonds may see selling pressure. Medium-term · 1–5d Over 1-5 trading days, expect continued equity volatility with growth stocks underperforming, further USD upside, and potential spillover into credit spreads and emerging market currencies. The US Treasury market has crossed a threshold that had stood for years, and it is showing no inclination to turn back. Yields across the curve have pushed past levels unseen in decades, marking a psychological break for a market that anchors global borrowing costs. The significance extends well beyond the bond market itself: Treasuries set the risk-free benchmark against which equities, corporate credit, mortgages and currencies are priced, so a sustained move higher in yields transmits directly into the cost of capital for households, companies and governments alike. The brief from Bloomberg Markets is unambiguous on the direction — the rise shows no sign of slowing. The backdrop matters. Treasury yields are driven principally by expectations for central bank policy, the inflation outlook, the pace of government borrowing and the term premium investors demand for holding duration risk. When those forces align, as they appear to have done this year, yields can climb persistently rather than mean-revert. The crossing of multi-decade barriers is itself consequential, because technical levels in the bond market often shape positioning: once breached, they can trigger stop-outs, force reassessments of duration exposure and draw in momentum-driven selling that reinforces the original move. Comparable episodes offer a rough guide. Periods of rapidly rising yields have historically compressed equity valuations, particularly for long-duration growth assets whose cash flows sit far in the future, and have widened credit spreads as refinancing costs rise. They have also tended to strengthen the dollar by attracting yield-seeking capital, while pressuring emerging-market borrowers who fund themselves in hard currency. The current move differs from a simple growth-driven rise in that the brief points to a broad, multi-maturity shift rather than an isolated move at one part of the curve — a sign that the repricing is about the whole term structure, not a single data point. For markets, the implications are analytical rather than prescriptive. Higher long-end yields raise the discount rate applied to every asset, which mechanically lowers the present value of future cash flows. That tends to weigh on rate-sensitive sectors and on any borrower facing rollover. At the same time, higher yields restore income to fixed-income portfolios, which can attract buyers back into the asset class after years of poor carry. The tension between those two effects — valuation compression versus improved income — is likely to define cross-asset performance while the move runs its course. The absence of any sign of slowing means positioning that assumed a ceiling on yields is the most exposed. The move also carries fiscal and policy implications. Sustained increases in Treasury yields raise the government's own cost of servicing debt, a feedback loop that can influence issuance decisions and, at the margin, the political appetite for further borrowing. For the Federal Reserve, a persistent rise in long-end yields does some of the tightening work on its behalf, but it can also signal concerns about inflation or fiscal credibility that the central bank cannot ignore. The brief does not attribute the move to a single cause, and market participants are likely to treat it as the product of several forces operating at once. What comes next will be read through a handful of channels. Investors will watch whether the rise continues across maturities or concentrates at the long end, since the shape of the curve carries different information in each case. They will track inflation and policy signals for confirmation or contradiction of the move's drivers, and monitor credit spreads and equity valuations for signs that higher discount rates are feeding through. Flows into and out of bond funds, the dollar's response, and the tone of Treasury auctions will all serve as gauges of whether buyers are stepping in or standing back. For now, the market's message is one-directional: the barrier has been crossed, and the climb has not stopped.

results.title: Goldman Sachs says the AI selloff is a rotation, not a liquidation
highlights: Goldman Sachs says the AI selloff is a rotation, not a liquidation Goldman Sachs says the AI selloff is a rotation, not a liquidation Goldman's Rich Privorotsky argues investors are reshuffling AI bets, not abandoning them, as memory chip stocks slide by Diego Almada Lopez Oct. 13, 2026 AI stocks just had a rough stretch, and memory chipmakers took the worst of it. Goldman Sachs is telling clients not to read it as a mass exit. Rich Privorotsky, who heads EMEA delta-one at Goldman Sachs, said on October 13, 2026, that the unwind looks like a rotation rather than a liquidation. In his telling, investors are moving money around inside the AI trade, not walking away from it. The trouble reportedly traced back to weakness at CXMT, a Chinese memory manufacturer, around October 12. What started in one corner of the chip world did not stay there for long. The KOSPI fell 5.5%. Samsung dropped 8%, SK Hynix slid 10%, and Kioxia took the heaviest hit with a 13% decline. The pain carried over to the SOXX semiconductor index, which was under pressure and potentially headed for a sixth consecutive down day. The most telling data point came from futures markets. Nasdaq futures fell approximately 70 basis points, while Russell futures rose around 30 basis points. In a true liquidation, investors tend to sell everything they can to raise cash, and indexes usually fall together. Here, money appeared to be leaving one part of the market and landing in another. Goldman has framed the volatility as a healthy reset for the AI space. The bank’s view is that positioning had become overly crowded during a period of high volatility, which left the trade vulnerable to a sharp shakeout. Hedge fund data cited in Goldman’s commentary shows funds have cut back substantially on technology exposure. At the same time, they have kept robust positions in a select group of mega-cap stocks. In July 2026, Goldman’s analysis described an earlier round of tech selling as the largest in a decade, yet characterized the move as a tactical adjustment rather than a loss of conviction in the AI investment thesis. The pattern since then has been a shift within AI itself. Money has been moving away from semiconductors and hardware and toward software, infrastructure, and higher-quality names. Hedge funds trimming broad tech exposure while holding onto the largest names means the trade is narrowing, not disappearing. Memory and semiconductor names face a tougher question. The declines at Samsung, SK Hynix, and Kioxia show how quickly sentiment can turn when weakness surfaces at one manufacturer like CXMT. The Nasdaq versus Russell divergence is the other gauge worth tracking. If that gap persists, it would support Goldman’s view that money is being redistributed rather than pulled from the market entirely. If both indexes start falling together, the rotation thesis gets harder to defend. Disclosure: This article was edited by Diego Almada Lopez. results.title: Weekly market commentary
highlights: Market take Weekly video_20261012 Wei Li Global Chief Investment Strategist BlackRock SCRIPT Camera frame Title slide: Upgrading U.S. Treasuries to lock in income This week we are making some tactical view changes, in particular changing our views on U.S. Treasuries and U.S. equities. 1: Locking in U.S. Treasury income Starting with U.S. Treasuries, we first went underweight U.S. long-duration Treasuries back in October 2020, when the U.S. 10-year [yield] was still below 0.9%. Since then, we have had brief periods of neutral but stayed mostly underweight. The U.S. 10-year [yield] is now at five and a quarter [5.25%], and we are upgrading to neutral to lock in income. We’re refraining from making a bigger bullish call on the long end of the U.S. Treasuries market and instead are upgrading front-end Treasuries into overweight, given the greater income buffer for further yield increases. 2: Downgrading U.S. equities On U.S. equities, we are bringing overweight to neutral, partly funding the Treasuries upgrade. We still prefer AI and tech within the neutral stance. This is a short-term risk management move, really reflecting the fact that we believe investors need to be more dynamic in this new market and macro regime. 3: A more dynamic approach Our conviction in the fundamentals remains intact, and we stand ready to add risk on potentially more attractive venture points. Other adjustments include trimming our Japanese government bond underweight, after Japanese 10-year [yields] rose from [around] 0.4% when we first initiated the position in mid-2023 to now around 3%. Outro: Here’s our Market take The big picture is that the new investment regime requires a very dynamic approach. We are managing risk, not changing our core convictions. Closing frame: Read details: blackrock.com/weekly-commentary We upgrade U.S. Treasuries, preferring short-term bonds, as higher yields improve potential returns, partly funded by downgrading U.S. equities to neutral. Global bonds swung sharply last week, with 10- and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields hitting 24-year highs before retreating after strong bond auctions. U.S. CPI and PPI offer the first look at September inflation this week. We watch for signs that could shift Fed expectations and Treasury yields. Higher yields and potentially excessive Fed tightening expectations create room to unwind our U.S. Treasury underweight – a mainstay for most of the last six years. We upgrade Treasuries, favoring short-term bonds. In turn, we take profits: downgrading U.S. equities to neutral to manage potential volatility around the AI buildout and trimming our Japanese government bond (JGB) underweight. We retain our conviction in AI fundamentals and preference for AI within U.S. equities. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen 110 basis points this year to around 5.25%, driven mainly by higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations or term premium. Two forces are behind the rise in real rates: intensifying competition for capital is pushing up the neutral rate while Middle East tensions and higher oil prices have driven a sharp reversal in Fed rate expectations. Since January, markets have priced in 160 additional basis points of Fed tightening over the next 12 months. We think that is overdone. With term premium averaging around 75 basis points since September, higher yields offer a more attractive entry point. At current yields, our analysis suggests a 75-basis-point cushion against further yield increases over 12 months before total returns turn negative. That supports adding U.S. Treasuries, especially at the short end, where we see the greatest scope for Fed tightening expectations to unwind. We are adding Treasuries from across the curve. For most of the last six years, we’ve been underweight Treasuries, turning neutral in spots. Now, yields have reset toward our long-held higher-rates view, and we want to lock in some attractive income. Ten-year Treasury yields sat near 0.9% back in October 2020 when we first went underweight and have since surged to 24-year highs above 5.3%. We are upgrading shorter-term Treasuries to overweight, where we see scope for excessive Fed tightening expectations to unwind, and long-term Treasuries to neutral as higher yields now provide better compensation for interest-rate risk. We also trim our underweight in JGBs, held since July 2023 when 10-year yields were at 0.4%-0.5%, compared with above 3% now. We fund the Treasury upgrades partly from U.S. agency mortgage-backed securities that have been a stable source of income in portfolios and we are now neutral. We also fund the Treasury upgrades by closing our long-held U.S. equity overweight to neutral. This is a short-term risk-management move, reflecting our belief that investors must be more dynamic in today’s volatile macro and market regime. We are also monitoring growing focus on AI policy and the AI buildout in jurisdictions across the country. Our fundamental convictions on AI transformation remain intact. Higher rates are increasingly differentiating companies by their ability to generate earnings and returns above the cost of capital. We still favor AI-related companies and listed infrastructure, where growing demand and scarcity in critical infrastructure support attractive returns. Existing infrastructure could grow even more valuable amid this scarcity. Despite narrative swings, we believe fundamentals will ultimately prevail. We also maintain our emerging market equity overweight. FactSet data shows third-quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are expected to grow nearly 30% year-on-year. We are managing near-term risk, not changing our core convictions. Higher yields offer an opportunity to add Treasuries, funded partly by taking profits on U.S. equities. We remain constructive on AI and stand ready to add risk again as visibility improves and attractive entry points emerge. Global government bonds saw another volatile week, with 10- and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields hitting their highest levels since 2002 before retreating after strong bond auctions. European bonds also sold off, led by France amid fiscal concerns. Oil prices rose as Middle East tensions persisted, adding to inflation worries. We see the bond selloff as reinforcing our competition-for-capital thesis, while higher yields improve the case for owning Treasuries. U.S. CPI and PPI data take center stage this week, offering the first snapshots of September inflation. Fed minutes last week underscored caution about the policy path and the importance of incoming data. We are watching for persistent price pressures amid higher energy costs and recent PCE methodology changes, with the readings likely to shape Fed rate expectations and Treasury yields.

results.title: Why Stocks and Bonds are RALLYING After Fed Rate Hike! (Market Update) (2026)
highlights: and Bonds are RALLYING If you had asked me yesterday what the market reaction to a Federal Reserve interest rate hike would be, I probably would have predicted a bloodbath. Logic suggests that when the cost of borrowing goes up, equity valuations go down. Yet, Thursday morning saw a completely different reality: stocks soared, bonds rallied, and investors seemed to be throwing a party. It is a classic example of how market psychology often defies basic economic textbook rules, and personally, I find this disconnect absolutely fascinating. What we witnessed wasn't just a reaction to numbers on a screen; it was a massive vote of confidence in a new era of central banking leadership. The market isn't reacting to the rate hike itself, but rather to the person wielding the hammer. One thing that immediately stands out to me is the sheer impact of Kevin Warsh’s communication style. After a period of confusion where bond yields spiked to multi-decade highs, leaving investors grasping at straws, Warsh stepped into the spotlight and provided something the markets crave more than anything else: clarity. By delivering a press conference that was described as "coherent" and "consistently hawkish," he effectively ended the guessing game. From my perspective, this is the most critical takeaway from the day. What many people don't realize is that markets can actually price in uncertainty much more easily than they can price in a known, albeit painful, reality. When the Fed is indecisive, volatility explodes. By being "hawkish without being crazy," as one analyst put it, Warsh has managed to "thread the needle." Personally, I think this suggests we are entering a phase where the Fed's greatest asset isn't its ability to move rates, but its ability to manage expectations. This is a huge shift from the era of "transparency" that often felt more like "constant surprises." Furthermore, the fact that the Fed chose to defy the political pressure from the Trump administration to hike rates is a detail I find especially interesting. It signals that the institution is fighting to preserve its independence. If the Fed loses its reputation as an autonomous body, the long-term implications for global bond markets would be catastrophic. This move wasn't just about inflation; it was about institutional survival. While the Fed provided the psychological floor, the cooling of oil prices provided the actual fuel for the rally. Seeing U.S. crude dip below the $100 mark is a significant psychological milestone. What makes this particularly fascinating is the cocktail of geopolitical factors driving this decline. We are seeing a convergence of potential diplomacy—specifically the rumors of President Trump discussing the Iran situation with Gulf leaders—and the physical reality of Saudi Arabia potentially restoring its pipeline capacity. If you take a step back and think about it, the market is essentially betting on a de-escalation of the "geopolitical risk premium." For months, oil has been trading at a premium not just because of supply and demand, but because of the fear of sudden, violent disruptions. When that fear recedes, even slightly, it acts like a massive shot of adrenaline for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. However, I must offer a word of caution: despite this dip, oil prices are still up over 65% since the start of the year. This rally feels like a relief valve being opened, not a permanent end to the era of high energy costs. Despite the green numbers on the tickers, I can't help but feel a sense of underlying fragility in this rally. This raises a deeper question: is this a genuine recovery, or just a momentary sigh of relief before the next wave of pain? - The "Higher for Longer" Reality: Fed officials have already signaled that more hikes are likely before the year ends. We aren't at the peak; we are likely just climbing the mountain. - The Diesel Disconnect: While crude is dipping, retail diesel prices have surged nearly 93% in a month. This is a massive drag on the real economy that won't show up in a stock index rally until it's too late. - Global Contagion: The Bank of Japan is expected to move on interest rates very soon. In our hyper-connected global economy, a move in Tokyo can trigger a massive liquidation in New York. What this really suggests is that the market is currently in a state of "hopeful denial." It is celebrating the clarity of the Fed and the dip in oil, while simultaneously ignoring the fact that the fundamental cost of doing business is still rising. In my opinion, we are seeing a market that is highly sensitive to sentiment but remains dangerously exposed to the structural reality of inflation. Ultimately, Thursday was a masterclass in how markets interpret leadership. The rally wasn't an endorsement of high interest rates; it was an endorsement of a predictable central bank. But we must be careful not to mistake predictability for stability. The Fed is walking a tightrope, and while Kevin Warsh may have found his footing, the economic landscape beneath him remains incredibly volatile. Personally, I think investors should enjoy this rally, but they should do so with one eye firmly on the exit sign.

results.title: Intermarket Analysis: DXY, Bonds & Correlations Guide
highlights: | Correlation | Relationship | Trading Implication | | --- | --- | --- | | DXY vs Gold | Inverse (strong) | Rising DXY = headwind for Gold longs. Falling DXY = tailwind. | | DXY vs EUR/USD | Inverse (very strong) | DXY trending up = EUR/USD trending down. Check DXY before trading EUR. | | US yields vs USD | Positive | Rising yields attract capital to USD. Strengthens dollar, pressures Gold. | | Equities vs Risk currencies | Positive | Risk-on (stocks up) = AUD, NZD strengthen. Risk-off = JPY, CHF strengthen. | | BTC vs Risk sentiment | Positive (increasingly) | BTC trades as a risk asset. Equity selloffs drag BTC. Risk rallies lift it. | Global financial markets are built on four asset classes: equities (stocks), bonds (fixed income), commodities (gold, oil, agricultural products), and currencies (forex). Each reacts to economic conditions differently, and their interactions create a web of relationships that institutional traders monitor constantly. In a healthy, growing economy, equities tend to rise as corporate earnings increase. Bonds tend to fall as interest rates rise. Commodities tend to rise as demand increases. In a contracting economy, the relationships flip. Understanding which regime you are in — expansion or contraction — tells you which relationships to expect. If you trade only one intermarket relationship, make it the US Dollar Index. DXY measures the dollar’s strength against a basket of major currencies (primarily the Euro, which accounts for nearly 58% of the index). It is the single most important macro variable because nearly every asset in the world is priced, traded, or benchmarked against the dollar. When DXY strengthens, dollar-denominated commodities become more expensive for foreign buyers, which typically pressures prices lower. Emerging market currencies and assets also come under pressure. When DXY weakens, commodities tend to rise, emerging markets outperform, and risk appetite generally increases. The traditional relationship between bonds and equities is inverse: when stocks fall, bonds rise, and vice versa. This held reliably for most of the 2000s and 2010s. But in 2022, it broke — both stocks and bonds fell simultaneously as central banks raised rates aggressively. Correlations are not laws. They are tendencies that hold under certain macroeconomic conditions and break under others. The practical signal to watch is the US 10-Year Treasury yield. When the 10-Year yield rises sharply, growth stocks come under pressure because higher discount rates reduce the present value of future earnings. If you trade equity indices like the Nasdaq, the 10-Year yield is the most important single variable outside of the index itself. Gold’s relationship with interest rates is often misunderstood. Gold responds to real interest rates — the nominal rate minus inflation. When real yields are negative, gold tends to rise because holding cash loses purchasing power. When real yields are positive and rising, gold tends to struggle. Track this through TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) yields. The simplest intermarket framework is the risk-on/risk-off binary. In risk-on environments, capital flows into equities, high-yield bonds, commodity currencies (AUD, NZD, CAD), emerging markets, and Bitcoin. In risk-off environments, capital flows into US Treasuries, the US dollar, the Japanese yen, the Swiss franc, and gold. The VIX (CBOE Volatility Index) is the most widely used barometer. A low VIX (below 15–18) indicates complacency. A VIX spike above 25–30 typically coincides with aggressive risk-off moves across all asset classes. During extreme risk-off events, correlations tighten dramatically — assets that normally move independently begin moving together because the only trade that matters is reducing exposure. Bitcoin’s evolving relationship with the Nasdaq — its decoupling periods and why CME BTC futures track traditional risk sentiment more closely than spot — makes intermarket analysis particularly relevant for crypto traders. When DXY weakens and equities rally, crypto tends to follow. When the VIX spikes, crypto sells off alongside traditional risk assets. Before you open a single chart, check three things: DXY (which direction is the dollar moving?), bonds (is the 10-Year yield rising or falling?), and VIX (is volatility expanding or contracting?). If all three align with your trade thesis, proceed. If they conflict, proceed with caution or reduce size. If they directly oppose your thesis, step aside. Intermarket analysis is the study of how different financial markets (currencies, bonds, commodities, equities) influence each other. For traders, the most important correlations include: US Dollar Index (DXY) vs Gold (inverse), bond yields vs currency strength (positive for the issuing country), and equity indices vs risk sentiment (risk-on vs risk-off dynamics). Understanding these relationships provides directional context that pure chart analysis cannot. The US Dollar Index measures USD strength against a basket of major currencies. When DXY rises, USD-denominated pairs (EUR/USD, GBP/USD, AUD/USD) tend to fall. When DXY falls, they tend to rise. Gold also moves inversely to DXY. Checking DXY before trading USD pairs gives you a macro directional filter that supplements your market structure analysis. Gold is priced in USD. When the dollar strengthens, Gold becomes more expensive for holders of other currencies, reducing demand and pushing the price down. Additionally, Gold is a safe haven that competes with USD-denominated assets: when interest rates rise (strengthening USD), the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding Gold increases, making bonds more attractive by comparison. Rising bond yields in a country attract capital (higher returns), strengthening that country’s currency. Falling yields push capital out, weakening the currency. The US 10-year Treasury yield is particularly important: rising US yields tend to strengthen USD and weaken Gold. Central bank rate decisions directly influence bond yields, which is why economic calendar awareness matters. Not in detail, but a quick 2-minute check of DXY direction and US yields as part of your pre-session routine provides valuable context. If DXY is trending strongly up, your bullish Gold thesis has a headwind. If yields are collapsing, your USD longs face resistance. These macro filters take seconds to check and prevent trades that fight the broader flow.

results.title: Market Quick Take: Bond Yields Hit 24-Year Highs, Euro Slides & Nasdaq Record (2026)
highlights: Market Quick Take: Bond Yields Hit 24-Year Highs, Euro Slides & Nasdaq Record (2026) Have you ever looked at financial headlines and felt like you were watching a movie where two completely contradictory plot lines are happening at the exact same time? Personally, I think today's market environment is the ultimate manifestation of that feeling. On one hand, bond yields are scaling heights we haven't seen in nearly a quarter of a century. On the other hand, tech equities like the Nasdaq are aggressively punching through all-time records, while major global currencies like the euro are quietly losing their footing. One thing that immediately stands out in the current landscape is the breathtaking ascent of bond yields, touching levels not witnessed in 24 years. If you take a step back and think about it, traditional financial theory tells us this should be kryptonite for growth stocks. Higher yields mean higher borrowing costs, heavier debt-servicing burdens, and a more expensive future discounted cash flow. Yet, the Nasdaq continues to shatter records anyway. While equity traders pop champagne over record highs, the currency market tells a far more sobering story. The euro’s recent slide against the dollar highlights a growing divergence in economic momentum and institutional confidence across borders. A weak currency is never just a line on a forex chart; it is a cultural and economic mirror reflecting a region's relative appeal to global capital. suggests is that capital voting with its feet, fleeing sluggish growth zones and rushing toward regions perceived as more dynamic. One detail that I find especially interesting is how nonchalant everyday consumers are about currency depreciation until it suddenly shows up in the price of imported goods, energy, and travel We treat forex movements as abstract numbers for hedge funds, but they the quiet tax drains purchasing power from ordinary households. This raises a deeper question: are we becoming numb to financial extremes? When 24-year highs in bond yields and record-breaking tech rallies become routine Tuesday morning news, it tells me that our collective threshold for financial volatility has shifted dramatically. If you dig beneath the surface, these trends point to an era where market resilience is constantly being tested by shifting central bank policies and geopolitical tremors. People usually misunderstand these market fluctuations as random noise, but they are actually signals of a fundamental plumbing overhaul in how global wealth is allocated. What matters most isn't chasing every record-breaking index or panicking over every currency dip, but understanding the underlying structural forces at play. Personally, I believe the biggest risk isn't market volatility itself, but our willingness to accept extraordinary financial stress as just another ordinary day at the office.
